paragraphs.text: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 is a connective tissue disorder whose features overlap with Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Marfan syndrome, and Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome. Craniofacial findings include hypertelorism, bifid uvula, and cleft palate. Skeletal findings include arachnodactyly, joint hypermobility, pectus deformity, scoliosis, and clubfoot. Cardiovascular involvement includes thoracic and abdominal aortic aneurysm and dissection and mitral valve disease (Bertoli-Avella et al., 2015). Expression varies widely within and between families: some patients have no cardiovascular findings, and stature ranges from short to tall (Rienhoff et al., 2013; Bertoli-Avella et al., 2015; Kuechler et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) reported a 9-year-old European American girl born to healthy nonconsanguineous parents. At birth she had contractures of the right hand, most severe in the third and fourth fingers, and of all toes. She also had long, narrow-appearing hands and feet, a midline facial nevus flammeus, and mild hypotonia. Her birth weight was 2.9 kg (5th centile). At 3 months she was evaluated for failure to thrive and delayed gross motor function. At 17 months she weighed 7.5 kg (less than 1st centile) and was 76 cm tall (5th centile). Findings at that age included bilateral pes planus, mild pectus excavatum, hyperextensibility of multiple large joints, mild retrognathia, prominent eyes, hypertelorism, a bifid uvula with an intact hard palate, a small metopic ridge, and blue sclerae. She had decreased bulk in all appendicular and axial muscles, strength of 1/5, low tone, diminished reflexes, and markedly reduced subcutaneous fat. She stood independently with a positive Gower sign at 20 months and walked at 24 months with a 'hip waddle.' Her neurocognitive development was appropriate for age. Radiographs showed bilateral coxa valga. At age 7 years she weighed 15.5 kg (less than 1st centile) and was 115 cm tall (5th centile), with marked hyperextensibility of the elbows and knees. A quadriceps muscle biopsy at that age showed type 1 fiber predominance with mild, focal type 1 fiber disproportion consistent with disuse, without dystrophic or inflammatory changes. Yearly echocardiograms from 18 months onward showed no cardiac defect or dysfunction. At 6.5 years, aortic annulus and aortic root dimensions were normal. The authors noted overlap with Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, and Beals-Hecht syndromes, but the patient did not meet diagnostic criteria for any of them.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) studied a large Dutch family (family 1) with clinical features overlapping Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes. Seven family members, aged 40 to 68 years, had aneurysms and dissections mainly involving the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta. Three died from aortic dissection and rupture. Four family members had mitral valve abnormalities, ranging from mild prolapse to severe regurgitation requiring surgery. Craniofacial abnormalities were subtle and included a long face, high-arched palate, and retrognathia. Pectus deformity and scoliosis were frequent. Other recurrent findings were velvety skin, varices, and hiatal hernia. Several family members had autoimmune features, including HLA-B27-positive spondyloarthritis, Graves disease, and celiac disease. Pathology reports from 2 deceased patients described extensive elastic fiber fragmentation and aortic medial degeneration.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) identified 10 further families with TGFB3 mutations, giving a total of 43 patients from 11 families. The phenotypes overlapped significantly with Loeys-Dietz syndrome. Vascular involvement ranged from no cardiovascular abnormalities at age 64 years to type A aortic dissection (median age, 51 years; range, 40 to 80) or type B aortic dissection (median age, 44.5 years; range, 30 to 57). It also included abdominal aortic dissection, and 1 patient died from cerebral aneurysm dissection at age 55. The authors observed no early arterial dissections and no dissections at small aortic dimensions. Other cardiovascular features were mitral valve disease, persistent foramen ovale, and atrial or ventricular septal defects. Iliac and subclavian artery aneurysms were found in 2 patients, and no striking arterial tortuosity was seen. Systemic features included tall stature (12 patients), arachnodactyly (16), pectus deformity (8), kyphoscoliosis (11), joint hypermobility (9), hypertelorism (14), bifid uvula (11), and cleft palate (5). Cervical spine instability, clubfoot, dolichocephaly, high-arched palate, retrognathia, and inguinal hernia also occurred. No ectopia lentis was documented, and early-onset osteoarthritis was reported in only 2 individuals. One patient had short stature and received growth hormone during puberty. The aortic wall of 1 patient showed elastic fiber fragmentation with increased collagen and proteoglycan deposition. The authors noted striking intrafamilial and interfamilial variability: some patients had typical LDS features and others had none.
